name: Bill Hagerty
bio: Former U.S. Ambassador to Japan and Tennessee Commissioner of Economic and Community Development. Trump-endorsed; $5.3M cash on hand.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Hagerty has no specific 2026 statements on pre-K or Head Start. His February 2026 Senate floor remarks praised Tennessee's school choice expansion but made no mention of early childhood programs. The OBBB he supported (July 2025) quadrupled the employer childcare tax credit but did not expand direct pre-K or Head Start funding.
early_childhood_ed.details: On February 5, 2026, Hagerty praised Governor Lee's State of the State address from the Senate floor, emphasizing parental school choice and noting Tennessee has risen to a top-5 state for reading and math gains — but framed entirely around K-12 school choice, with no mention of pre-K or Head Start. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act he voted for in July 2025 quadrupled the employer childcare credit, which advocacy groups note primarily benefits higher-income working parents with employer-sponsored childcare rather than low-income families. No bill sponsorships or floor statements specifically addressing Head Start, universal pre-K, or childcare deserts have been identified in 2026. Tennessee's federal Child Care Development Fund allocation was cut by $44.5 million for FY2025, but Hagerty issued no public response.

child_hunger.summary: Hagerty voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (July 2025), which enacted the largest SNAP cuts in the program's history — approximately $187 billion over 10 years. As of May 30, 2026, at least 3.5 million Americans had lost SNAP access nationally; Tennessee lost approximately 16% of SNAP enrollment. Advocacy groups demonstrated outside his Nashville office; his office did not respond to media requests for comment on Tennessee impacts.
child_hunger.details: The OBBB, which Hagerty voted for on July 1, 2025 (Senate passed 51-50 with VP Vance casting the tiebreaker), cut SNAP by $187 billion over a decade. New work requirements now extend to adults ages 55-64 and parents of children 14 and up. States with error rates above 6% must now cover up to 15% of benefit costs, putting Tennessee on the hook for an estimated $110 million+ annually. CNBC reported on May 30, 2026 that 3.5 million Americans nationally have lost SNAP access since July 2025, with Tennessee seeing roughly a 16% decline in SNAP enrollment. Advocacy groups including the Chattanooga Area Food Bank and Tennessee Caregiver Coalition held demonstrations outside Hagerty's Nashville office urging a no vote before passage. WBIR and WKRN reported that Hagerty's office did not respond to requests for comment on the Tennessee fiscal impact.

parental_support.summary: The OBBB Hagerty voted for raised the Child Tax Credit to $2,200 per child (permanent, inflation-indexed), quadrupled the employer childcare credit, created a PFML credit, and established Trump Accounts. However, the CTC expansion does not increase benefits for the estimated 17 million children in families too poor to claim the full credit. His February 2026 floor remarks emphasized parental rights in education and school choice rather than economic supports for parents.
parental_support.details: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act included a CTC increase to $2,200 per child (permanent and inflation-indexed); analysis by the Tax Policy Center notes neither the House nor Senate plans increased refundability for the ~17 million lowest-income children who currently receive less than the $2,000 maximum credit. Hagerty's February 5, 2026 Senate floor statement focused on school choice and parental rights in education, noting Tennessee received 54,000 applications for 20,000 Education Freedom Scholarship spots. He framed the OBBB in a June 30, 2025 Bloomberg TV appearance primarily as a tax cut and anti-tax-increase measure. The quadrupled employer childcare credit and PFML credit in OBBB are supply-side mechanisms that primarily benefit employers and higher-income families with employer-sponsored benefits.

name: Marquita Bradshaw
bio: Memphis environmental justice activist who won the 2020 Democratic primary against expectations. Running again on environmental and economic-justice platform.
photo_credit: Bradshaw for Senate official campaign website

early_childhood_ed.summary: Bradshaw supports high-quality public education for every child from pre-K through 12th grade as a core campaign platform plank, including universal pre-K and quality childcare. No new 2025-2026 specific statements beyond her campaign website positions were found.
early_childhood_ed.details: Bradshaw's campaign website at marquitabradshaw.com reflects support for universal pre-K, quality childcare, and high-quality public education from pre-K through grade 12. Her signature framing — 'I am a lifelong proponent of funding our education system the same as we do our military' — appears on her current issues page. Her 2020 platform explicitly listed 'Fund universal pre-K education' and 'Provide quality childcare.' As a single working-class mother who raised her son in Memphis, she has drawn personal connections between access to childcare and economic opportunity. No 2025-2026 press releases or campaign announcements specifically addressing Head Start funding levels or childcare cost legislation were found.

child_hunger.summary: No specific 2025-2026 public statements from Bradshaw on child hunger, SNAP, Summer EBT, or school nutrition programs were found. Her broader platform emphasizes working-class economic justice and healthcare access.
child_hunger.details: Research through June 2026 found no press releases, social media posts, or campaign statements from Marquita Bradshaw specifically addressing SNAP, Summer EBT, child hunger, or school nutrition programs. This is notable given the significant Tennessee-specific child hunger debate: Governor Lee's decision to opt out of the $84 million federal Summer EBT program for a second consecutive summer (affecting roughly 700,000 children), the OBBB's $187 billion SNAP cut package, and bipartisan state-level pushback including the $7 million budget allocation for S-EBT in 2027. Bradshaw's OnTheIssues Families & Children page shows no stance on record.

parental_support.summary: Bradshaw supports a $15 minimum wage, healthcare for all, and high-quality public education as her core economic support mechanisms for working families. No specific positions on paid family leave, the Child Tax Credit, or direct childcare cost programs were found in 2025-2026 research.
parental_support.details: Bradshaw's current campaign issues page calls for 'fully and aggressively fighting for the federal recognition and implementation of a living wage beginning at immediately increasing the minimum wage to $15.00 an hour.' Her 2020 platform included 'relieve current student debt, provide quality childcare' as part of her economic agenda. No 2025-2026 press releases or campaign statements addressing the OBBB's child tax credit provisions, federal paid leave legislation, or childcare affordability were found. OnTheIssues records no stance from Bradshaw on the child tax credit, paid family leave, or childcare cost subsidy programs.

name: Maria Brewer
bio: Longtime Tennessee Democratic Party staffer making her first run for federal office.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Brewer's campaign website explicitly lists support for early childhood education and pre-K access as part of her education platform. No details on funding levels, program specifics, or legislative proposals have been published.
early_childhood_ed.details: The issues page at mariabrewerforsenate.com states Brewer supports investing in 'early childhood education and pre-K access' as part of her education policy platform. No additional detail on Head Start, childcare deserts, childcare workforce, or funding mechanisms appears on her site. Her April 25, 2026 Loyal Opposition podcast appearance focused on healthcare and cost of living without addressing early childhood specifically. She is a former Tennessee Democratic Party Director of Party Affairs running in the August 6, 2026 Democratic primary.

child_hunger.summary: No specific position on child hunger, SNAP, or food assistance was found on Brewer's campaign website or in any 2026 public statements. Her platform addresses grocery affordability broadly but does not mention SNAP cuts or Summer EBT.
child_hunger.details: Brewer's campaign site discusses cost-of-living concerns and grocery affordability but does not specifically address SNAP, Summer EBT, or child hunger programs. She frames the issue as 'Trumpflation created by chaotic tariffs' rather than targeting specific food assistance programs. No press releases, media appearances, or social media posts from May-June 2026 on these topics were surfaced. No stated positions exist on the SNAP food restriction waiver effective July 31, 2026.

parental_support.summary: Brewer's campaign website indicates she supports families with young children keeping more take-home pay rather than waiting for annual tax credits, suggesting implicit support for immediate income support over CTC-style annual refunds. She supports doubling the minimum wage. No specific positions on paid family leave or childcare credits were found.
parental_support.details: The issues section of mariabrewerforsenate.com contains language that 'families with young children and low income need to keep their pay, not just get credits once a year,' which implies a preference for wage-based income supports over annual refundable tax credits like the CTC. She supports doubling the minimum wage as a mechanism to provide working parents more financial stability. No specific positions on paid family medical leave, employer childcare credits, or childcare subsidy programs appear on her site.
